candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — antimicrobial resistance mechanisms and treatment response
candidate.educational_objective: Explain that bacterial antibiotic resistance can arise through multiple microbial defense mechanisms—reduced entry, efflux, drug inactivation, target alteration, or pathway bypass—and that resistance belongs to the microorganism rather than the client's body.

options.A: Bacteria may restrict drug entry, pump the drug out, enzymatically change or destroy it, alter its target, or bypass the drug's effect.
options.B: Antibiotic resistance occurs because the client's body becomes resistant to the medication rather than because the microorganism changes.
options.C: All resistant bacteria use the same defense mechanism, so identifying the antibiotic class predicts the exact resistance mechanism.
options.D: Resistance develops only after a bacterium has personally been exposed to the antibiotic; resistance traits cannot spread between microorganisms.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. CDC describes several antimicrobial-resistance mechanisms, including restricting antibiotic access, pumping the drug out, changing or destroying the drug with enzymes, changing the drug target, and bypassing the drug's effects. B is incorrect because antimicrobial resistance refers to the germ's ability to defeat the drug; it does not mean the patient's body has become resistant. C is incorrect because microorganisms can use multiple different resistance mechanisms. D is incorrect because resistance traits encoded in microbial DNA can spread to other germs, including germs that were not themselves exposed to the antimicrobial. Appropriate antibiotic use helps limit selection pressure and spread, but antibiotic exposure is not the only way a resistant organism can acquire a resistance trait.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Bacteria can resist antibiotics through several distinct microbial mechanisms, including reduced access, efflux, enzymatic drug modification/destruction, target alteration, and pathway bypass; resistance traits can spread between germs and do not represent resistance of the patient's body.
candidate.source_document_title: About Antimicrobial Resistance; How Antimicrobial Resistance Happens
candidate.source_locator: About Antimicrobial Resistance — 'How antimicrobial resistance happens' and 'Spread of germs and resistance mechanisms': resistance mechanisms include restricting antibiotic access, getting rid of antibiotics through pumps, changing or destroying antibiotics with enzymes, changing antibiotic targets, and bypassing antibiotic effects; resistant germs can share resistance mechanisms with other germs. '5 things to know': antimicrobial resistance means germs defeat antimicrobial drugs; it does not mean the body is resistant to them. How Antimicrobial Resistance Happens — At a glance: drug resistance occurs when bacteria no longer respond to the drug designed to kill them.
